title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022
source: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, clauses 4 to 10 and Annex A (reference numbers and official short titles)
licence: Reference numbers with the official short titles only; not the text of the standard. Purpose, guidance, audit questions and typical evidence are our own words. Buy the standard for the requirements.

requirements.title: Clause 4 · Context of the organization
requirements.purpose: Sets the ground for the whole system: what the organisation does, who cares about its information, and what the management system covers.

requirements.title: Understanding the organization and its context
requirements.purpose: Makes sure the security programme is shaped by the real situation of the business rather than a generic template.
requirements.guidance: List the internal and external factors that could help or hurt your ability to protect information: market, regulation, technology, ownership, culture, staffing, key suppliers. Since Amendment 1 of 2024 you must also decide whether climate change matters to your management system, for example flood risk to a data centre or energy costs for hosting; a reasoned conclusion that it does not is acceptable. A one or two page analysis that someone senior has read is enough for a small company. Review it at planned intervals, most organisations do so at least yearly, and show that it feeds risk assessment and objectives. A common pitfall is a copied SWOT that never mentions security.
questions: How did you decide which external and internal issues matter to your security programme?
When did you last review this list and what changed?
Show me where an issue on this list influenced a risk or an objective.
Who owns keeping the context analysis current?
How did you decide whether climate change is relevant to your security programme, and what did you conclude?
evidence: Context analysis or issues register with date and owner
Meeting minutes where the issues were discussed
Links from the issues to risks or objectives
Recorded decision on the relevance of climate change, with reasons

requirements.title: Understanding the needs and expectations of interested parties
requirements.purpose: Identifies who has a stake in your information security and which of their requirements you have chosen to meet.
requirements.guidance: Build a short table of interested parties such as customers, regulators, employees, owners, insurers and key suppliers, with what each expects and which of those expectations are legal or contractual. Mark which ones the management system will address. Keep customer contract clauses and regulatory duties traceable to this list. Since Amendment 1 of 2024 the standard notes that parties may have climate-related requirements, such as sustainability clauses in customer contracts, so check for them and record any you find. Auditors often find parties listed without any requirements, or requirements never reviewed after a new big customer signed.
questions: Who are your interested parties and what do they require from you?
Which of these requirements are legal or contractual obligations?
How do you learn about new customer security demands?
Where are these requirements reflected in your controls?
Do any interested parties have climate-related requirements, and how did you check?
evidence: Interested parties register with requirements and owner
Extracts of customer contracts or questionnaires mapped to requirements

requirements.title: Determining the scope of the information security management system
requirements.purpose: Draws a clear boundary around what the management system covers so that effort and certification claims are accurate.
requirements.guidance: Write a scope statement naming the services, sites, teams, systems and data included, and be explicit about what is outside and why. Base the boundary on what you found under 4.1 and 4.2, and show where your work hands over to suppliers, group companies or customers, because those hand-offs are where gaps hide. Keep the wording identical on the certificate application, the website and the internal document. Typical findings are scopes that exclude a cloud platform the product depends on, or that do not match the real organisation chart.
questions: What exactly is in scope and what is excluded?
Why is each exclusion justified, and who approved the scope?
How do dependencies on suppliers and other sites fit in the boundary?
Does the scope statement match what you tell customers?
evidence: Approved scope statement with version and date
Diagram of sites, systems and data flows in scope

requirements.title: Information security management system
requirements.purpose: Requires the organisation to actually run a management system, with processes that fit together and are improved over time.
requirements.guidance: Document how the main processes interact: risk management, control operation, incident handling, audit, review and improvement. A simple process map and a named owner per process are normally enough. The system must be maintained, not built once for the audit. Auditors check that records show the cycle running in practice, for example risk reviews, audits and management reviews happening on schedule.
questions: Which processes make up your management system and how do they connect?
Who owns each process and how do you know it is working?
Show me evidence of the system running over the last twelve months.
How do you decide when the system needs to change?
evidence: Records from the most recent cycle of each activity

requirements.title: Clause 5 · Leadership
requirements.purpose: Makes senior management visibly responsible for the security programme, its direction and its resources.

requirements.title: Leadership and commitment
requirements.purpose: Ensures senior leaders drive security, back it with resources and tie it to business goals.
requirements.guidance: Leaders should be able to explain, in their own words, why security matters to the business and what they have decided. Show it through approved budgets, attendance at management reviews, policy sign-off and removal of blockers. Avoid the pattern where the security lead does everything and management only signs at audit time. Interviews with directors are a standard audit step, so brief them on what they have actually approved.
questions: What has top management personally decided or approved about security this year?
How are security objectives linked to business strategy?
How do you make sure resources are available?
How is the importance of security communicated to staff?
evidence: Management review minutes with attendees and decisions
Approved security budget or resource plan

requirements.title: Policy
requirements.purpose: Gives the organisation a top-level statement of direction that everyone can follow and be held to.
requirements.guidance: Publish a short policy signed off by top management that fits what the business actually does, sets out what you are aiming for in security or how those aims are set, and promises both to meet the requirements that apply to you and to keep getting better. Keep it under document control, make sure staff have really received it, and share it with customers, suppliers or others when they have a reason to see it. Review it on a set cycle and whenever the business changes significantly. Keep it readable rather than a copy of the standard. Common findings are an unsigned or outdated policy, or one that staff have never seen.
questions: Who approved the policy and when was it last reviewed?
How is it communicated to staff and to outsiders who need it?
Where does the policy commit to objectives and improvement?
Can a random employee tell me what it says?
evidence: Approved policy with version, owner and date

requirements.title: Organizational roles, responsibilities and authorities
requirements.purpose: Makes sure each security duty has a named owner with the authority to act on it.
requirements.guidance: Define who is accountable for the management system, who reports on its performance to management, and who owns key processes. Record this in a role description or RACI and include deputies for absence. In small companies one person often holds several roles, which is acceptable if documented and realistic. Auditors test whether the named people know about their duties.
questions: Who is responsible for the overall system and for reporting to management?
How do people learn what is expected of them?
What happens when the security lead is absent?
Show me where authority to enforce a security rule is written down.
evidence: Roles and responsibilities document or RACI

requirements.title: Clause 6 · Planning
requirements.purpose: Covers how risks, opportunities, objectives and changes are planned so that the system achieves its aims.

requirements.title: Actions to address risks and opportunities
requirements.purpose: Frames the planning of risk work so that the system can reach its aims and prevent unwanted outcomes.
requirements.guidance: This is the umbrella for risk assessment and treatment. Use it to show that the issues from clause 4 and the needs of interested parties were turned into planned actions. Keep a simple link between context, risks and the actions you take. Auditors like to follow one thread from a context issue to a risk to a treatment to a control.
questions: How do context issues and stakeholder needs feed into your risk work?
Which opportunities, not only threats, have you considered?
Show me one risk traced to the action taken.
Which risk or opportunity changed your objectives or plans this year?
evidence: Traceability from issues to risks to actions
Action plans with owners and dates
Objectives or plans updated as a result of risk work

requirements.title: Planning for risks and opportunities
requirements.purpose: Ensures planning looks at what could stop the management system itself from delivering its intended results, and at chances to make it work better.
requirements.guidance: This is broader than the information security risk assessment in 6.1.2. Look at risks and opportunities for the management system as a whole, drawing on the issues from 4.1 and the requirements from 4.2: for example dependence on one security lead, a budget cut, a merger, a new certification demand from customers, or a tool that could automate evidence collection. Decide on actions, build them into existing processes such as projects, budgets and hiring rather than a separate list, and later check whether they worked. For a small company a short section in the risk procedure and a few entries in the register are enough. A frequent finding is an organisation that only records technical threats and has never considered risks to the system itself.
questions: Which risks to the management system itself, not only to information, have you identified?
What opportunities to improve the system did you find and act on?
Show me how one of these actions was built into a normal business process.
How did you judge whether the action achieved what you intended?
evidence: Risk procedure section covering management system risks and opportunities
Register entries for system-level risks and opportunities with owners
Project plans, budgets or hiring decisions that carry the actions
Effectiveness review notes or management review minutes

requirements.title: Information security risk assessment
requirements.purpose: Defines a repeatable way to find, analyse and rank information security risks.
requirements.guidance: Write a method that sets your risk criteria: scales for likelihood and consequence, the level at which a risk becomes acceptable, and how each risk gets an owner. Two people applying it to the same situation should reach roughly the same rating, so describe each point on the scales with concrete examples. Identify risks to the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information in scope; an asset-based approach is common, but scenario or process-based approaches are equally valid. Analyse each risk, compare it with the acceptance criteria and rank it for treatment, and keep both the method and the results on record. Pitfalls are scoring that depends on who did it, no risk owner sign-off, and assessments not repeated when something big changes.
questions: What criteria do you use to rate risk and who approved them?
How do you make sure two assessors reach similar results?
Who are risk owners and how did they confirm the ratings?
When and why do you repeat the assessment?
evidence: Risk assessment methodology with scales and acceptance criteria

requirements.title: Information security risk treatment
requirements.purpose: Turns assessed risks into decisions, chosen controls and a Statement of Applicability.
requirements.guidance: For each risk above your acceptance level, decide whether to reduce, avoid, share or accept it, and pick the controls that will do the job, from Annex A or any other source. Then check your selection against Annex A so nothing needed has been overlooked. The Statement of Applicability must list every control you need, say why each is included and whether it is in place yet, and give a reason for each Annex A control you leave out. Risk owners must approve the treatment plan and accept the leftover risk. Auditors check consistency between the register, the plan and the Statement of Applicability, and challenge exclusions that the risks clearly argue against.
questions: How did you pick controls for each risk?
Show me the Statement of Applicability: why is one control included, is it implemented, and why was another excluded?
Who approved the treatment plan and residual risk?
How do you track treatment actions to completion?
evidence: Risk treatment plan with owners and dates
Risk owner approval of residual risk

requirements.title: Information security objectives and planning to achieve them
requirements.purpose: Sets measurable goals for security and a plan for reaching them.
requirements.guidance: Choose a small number of objectives that can be measured, are consistent with the policy and take account of risk results. For each, state what will be done, who is responsible, what resources are needed, when it will finish and how success is judged. Typical examples are patching speed, training completion or incident response time. Auditors find objectives that are vague ('improve security') or never reviewed.
questions: What are your security objectives and how are they measured?
Who owns each and by when?
How do they relate to the policy and the risk results?
Show me the latest progress against one.
evidence: Objectives register with metrics, owners and dates

requirements.title: Planning of changes
requirements.purpose: Ensures changes to the management system itself are made in a planned and controlled way.
requirements.guidance: When you restructure processes, change scope, adopt new tools or reorganise teams, consider why, what the effect will be, who is involved and what resources are needed. A lightweight change record for the management system is sufficient. Distinguish this from technical change management, which is a control. Auditors look for evidence of one real change handled this way.
questions: Give an example of a recent change to the management system and how it was planned.
Who approves such changes?
How do you assess the effect on existing controls?
How do you record them?
evidence: Change record for an ISMS change

requirements.title: Clause 7 · Support
requirements.purpose: Covers the people, skills, communication and documents the system depends on.

requirements.title: Resources
requirements.purpose: Makes sure the system is given the people, time, tools and money it needs.
requirements.guidance: Show that resource needs are identified and met: budget lines, headcount or contractor time, tooling licences and training budget. Linking requests to risks and objectives makes the case persuasive. Auditors look at whether the person running the system has realistic time allocated and whether approved items were delivered.
questions: How do you decide what resources the system needs?
Who approves budget and what was approved last year?
Is the security lead's time formally allocated?
Show an example of a resource request that was granted or declined.

requirements.title: Competence
requirements.purpose: Ensures the people who affect security performance have the skills to do the job.
requirements.guidance: Define the skills needed for security roles such as the system owner, administrators and incident handlers, and compare them with what people have. Close gaps with training, mentoring or hiring, then keep records. For small teams a skills matrix plus training certificates works well. Auditors sample staff records and ask how you judged that training was effective.
questions: Which roles influence security and what skills do they need?
How do you verify people have them?
What did you do about a gap you found?
Where are the records kept?

requirements.title: Awareness
requirements.purpose: Makes everyone in scope understand the policy, their part and the effect of not following the rules.
requirements.guidance: This clause is about the result: people in scope know the security policy, understand how their own work helps or harms security, and know what follows if they ignore the rules. The training that gets them there is covered by control A.6.3, so here focus on checking that the message has landed. Test recall in team meetings, spot checks or short interviews, and pay particular attention to contractors and people who joined since the last campaign. Use what you find to adjust the programme. Auditors interview staff at random, so vague answers about the policy or about their own part in it are a common finding.
questions: What would a member of staff say if I asked what the security policy means for their job?
How do people learn how their own work affects security, for better or worse?
What do staff understand will happen if they do not follow the rules?
How do you check that contractors and recent joiners are aware, not just trained?
What changed after you found a gap in awareness?
evidence: Awareness messages explaining the policy and each person's contribution
Notes from spot interviews or recall checks
Awareness records for contractors and temporary staff
Actions taken after awareness gaps were found

requirements.title: Communication
requirements.purpose: Plans what security information is shared, with whom, when and how, inside and outside the organisation.
requirements.guidance: Create a simple communication matrix: topic, audience, owner, method and frequency. Include internal updates, customer notifications, regulator contacts, supplier notices and incident communications. Make sure there is a defined route for outside enquiries. Auditors check that the matrix is used, for example by showing a sent notice that matches it.
questions: Who decides what is communicated about security and to whom?
How do you handle a customer asking about an incident?
Show me the communication plan and an example of it being followed.
Who speaks for the organisation externally?

requirements.title: Documented information
requirements.purpose: Sets the expectation that the system keeps the documents and records it needs, and keeps them under control.
requirements.guidance: This clause groups the rules for what to write down, how to create and update it, and how to control it. Keep only what is useful: policies, procedures and records proving the system works. Over-documenting makes the system brittle. Auditors verify that documents referenced in the system actually exist and are current.
questions: What documented information have you decided you need and why?
How do you keep it current and available?
How do you stop obsolete versions being used?
Who owns the document set?

requirements.title: What must be documented
requirements.purpose: Requires the system to include the documents the standard asks for plus those the organisation decides it needs.
requirements.guidance: Start from what the standard explicitly asks you to keep: the scope, policy and objectives, the risk assessment and treatment processes, the Statement of Applicability and treatment plan, risk assessment and treatment results, evidence of competence, records showing operational processes ran as planned, monitoring results, the audit programme and audit results, management review results, and nonconformities with their corrective actions. Then add what your size, complexity and the competence of your people demand. Do not create documents just to look thorough. Auditors check each required item exists and is findable.
questions: Show me where each required document is.
How did you decide which extra documents were needed?
Who confirms the list is complete?
How do you decide when a process needs written instructions and when trained people are enough?
evidence: Document register mapped to required items
Index or table of contents of the system

requirements.title: Creating and updating
requirements.purpose: Ensures documents are identifiable, in a suitable format and approved before use.
requirements.guidance: Give every document a title, owner, version, date and approval. Use a standard template and a consistent location. Review at planned intervals and record the review even if nothing changes. Common findings are documents without owners, missing approval, or approval by the author alone.
questions: How are documents identified and approved?
Who reviews and how often?
Show me the history of one document.
What format and tools do you use?

requirements.title: Control of documented information
requirements.purpose: Keeps documents and records available when needed, protected, and under version control.
requirements.guidance: Store them in a controlled repository with defined access rights, backups and retention periods. Control distribution, changes and disposal. Handle documents from outside sources, such as supplier reports, in the same way. Auditors test whether staff can easily find the current version and whether records are protected against alteration.
questions: Where are documents stored and who can edit them?
How do you prevent use of old versions?
How long are records kept and how are they disposed of?
How is access to confidential documents restricted?
evidence: Backup or restore evidence for documents

requirements.title: Clause 8 · Operation
requirements.purpose: Covers running the planned processes, assessing risk on schedule and carrying out treatment.

requirements.title: Operational planning and control
requirements.purpose: Ensures the planned security processes are carried out as designed and outsourced activities are kept under control.
requirements.guidance: Set criteria for each key process, run the process to those criteria and keep enough records to show it happened as planned. This is also where the plans from clause 6, risk treatment and objectives, are actually carried out. Planned changes should follow a controlled route, and when something changes without a plan, look at what it did and limit any damage. Since 2022 the requirement covers any externally provided process, product or service that matters to the system, such as a managed service provider, a cloud platform or an outsourced help desk, not only outsourced processes. Auditors pick a process, such as access reviews, and ask for the last few records.
questions: Which processes keep the controls operating and what are their criteria?
How do you control externally provided processes, products and services that matter to security?
How do you handle unplanned changes?
Show me records from a recent run of a key process.
evidence: Register of externally provided processes, products and services with the controls applied

requirements.title: Information security risk assessment
requirements.purpose: Requires risk assessments to actually be carried out at planned intervals and when significant change occurs.
requirements.guidance: Keep a calendar for reassessment, normally at least annually, and define what counts as a trigger such as a new product, a major supplier or an incident. Retain the results each time. An assessment done once at certification and never repeated is a classic nonconformity.
questions: When was the last assessment and what triggered it?
What changed in the results compared with the previous one?
Who took part and who approved?
How do you handle a significant change between scheduled runs?
evidence: Updated risk register with revision history

requirements.title: Information security risk treatment
requirements.purpose: Requires the treatment plan to be put into practice and its results recorded.
requirements.guidance: Track each treatment action to completion with owner, date and proof, and update the register and Statement of Applicability as controls go live. Re-assess residual risk after treatment. Auditors compare the plan with the real state of controls and flag items that are long overdue.
questions: What is the status of the treatment plan?
Show me evidence that a planned control was implemented.
How do you handle overdue actions?
How is residual risk re-evaluated?
evidence: Implementation evidence such as configuration screenshots or approvals

requirements.title: Clause 9 · Performance evaluation
requirements.purpose: Covers measuring how well the system works, auditing it and reviewing it at management level.

requirements.title: Monitoring, measurement, analysis and evaluation
requirements.purpose: Provides evidence about whether the controls and processes are performing as intended.
requirements.guidance: Decide what to measure, how, how often, who analyses it and who sees the result. Pick a few useful metrics, for example patch age, access review completion, incident counts and training completion. Keep results and act on trends. Auditors reject metrics that are collected but never discussed.
questions: What do you measure and why?
Who reviews the results and how often?
Show me a case where a metric led to action.
How do you know the methods give valid results?

requirements.title: Internal audit
requirements.purpose: Checks, independently, whether the system meets requirements and is working in practice.
requirements.guidance: Establish an audit programme, use auditors who are not marking their own work and report results to management. Cover the whole system within the certification cycle, and focus more on higher risk areas. Auditors expect findings to be real; an audit with no findings invites suspicion.
questions: How does your audit coverage over the cycle span every clause, the controls in the Statement of Applicability and all sites in scope?
Show me the latest audit report and how its findings were closed.
What did internal audit tell management that it did not already know?
How are audit results used in management review?

requirements.title: Audits at planned intervals
requirements.purpose: Ensures internal audits test both whether the system meets your own rules and the standard, and whether it actually works in practice.
requirements.guidance: An internal audit has two jobs. The first is conformity: does the system meet ISO/IEC 27001 and what your own policies and procedures say. The second is effectiveness: are the controls and processes really operating and kept up, judged on records and observation rather than documents alone. Hold audits at planned intervals that suit your risks; most certified organisations cover the whole scope at least once in each three-year certification cycle and audit higher-risk areas every year. A frequent finding is an audit that only checks documents exist and never samples records.
questions: How do your audits check your own policies and procedures as well as the standard?
Show me where an audit tested that a control actually operates, not just that it is documented.
Were all audits planned for the last period completed, and if not, why?
How did you decide on the audit frequency for each area?
evidence: Audit checklists covering both the standard and internal procedures
Audit working papers with sampled records
Audit schedule showing planned and completed audits
Audit conclusions on conformity and effectiveness

requirements.title: Internal audit programme
requirements.purpose: Defines how audits are planned, run and reported so results are consistent and objective.
requirements.guidance: Write down how often each area is audited, how audits are carried out, who does them and how results are reported, and weight the plan towards processes that matter most or went wrong last time. For each audit record the criteria and scope. Pick auditors who do not audit their own work; small companies often use an external consultant or a peer from another team. Send results to the managers responsible and keep the plan, reports and evidence. A common gap is missing evidence of how scope or sampling was chosen.
questions: How is the programme prepared and who approves it?
How do past results influence what you audit next?
How do you ensure objectivity?
What criteria and scope did you set for the last audit, and how did you choose the sample?
evidence: Audit programme with frequency, methods and responsibilities
Audit plans with criteria, scope and sampling notes

requirements.title: Management review
requirements.purpose: Gives top management a regular, structured moment to judge whether the system is suitable and effective.
requirements.guidance: Hold reviews at planned intervals with a standard agenda and recorded decisions; most organisations meet at least yearly and many twice a year. Decisions on improvements, resources and changes should result in tracked actions. Leaders attending in person matters. Auditors read the minutes for decisions rather than just a list of topics.
questions: How does the review run, from preparing the pack to closing the actions?
What decisions were made?
How are review actions tracked?
How do you prepare the input?
evidence: Follow-up of review actions at the next review

requirements.title: Reviews at planned intervals
requirements.purpose: Requires top management itself to judge, on a planned schedule, whether the system still fits the business, is sufficient and works.
requirements.guidance: The review belongs to top management: the people with authority over budget and direction must take part, not only the security lead. Set the dates in advance, fitted to board or leadership cycles, and hold an extra review after a major change such as an acquisition or a serious incident. End the meeting with an explicit conclusion on whether the system still fits the business, covers what it needs to and delivers results. Auditors note skipped or delayed reviews, and reviews held without anyone from top management.
questions: Which members of top management took part in the last review?
Were all planned reviews held on time, and what happened when one slipped?
What did management conclude about whether the system still fits the business?
What would trigger an extra review outside the schedule?
evidence: Management review schedule aligned with the leadership calendar
Attendance list showing top management participation
Recorded conclusion on suitability, adequacy and effectiveness
Record of any extra review held after a major change

requirements.title: Management review inputs
requirements.purpose: Specifies the information leaders must be given so the review is informed.
requirements.guidance: Build the pack under fixed headings so nothing is skipped: progress on actions from the last review; what has changed in the business and its environment, and in what interested parties want from you (a heading added in 2022); how security is performing, shown as trends in nonconformities and corrective actions, metrics, audit findings and progress on objectives; feedback from customers and others; the current risk picture and where treatment stands; and ideas for improvement. Send it before the meeting so leaders can read it. A pack that omits audit results, incidents or progress on objectives is a typical weakness.
questions: What information do you prepare for the review?
Where do audit and incident results appear?
How do you show changes in what interested parties need from you?
Do you include feedback from customers?
Who compiles the pack?

requirements.title: Management review results
requirements.purpose: Ensures the review ends with decisions about improvement and changes to the system.
requirements.guidance: Record decisions on opportunities for improvement, changes needed to the system, resource needs and objectives. Convert each into an action with an owner and a date, and follow up at the next review. Keep the minutes as retained evidence. Reviews that finish with 'noted' for everything raise questions.
questions: What did the last review decide?
How were decisions turned into actions?
Were resource requests approved?
How do you track completion?
evidence: Updated objectives or policy after review

requirements.title: Clause 10 · Improvement
requirements.purpose: Covers fixing problems properly and steadily making the system better.

requirements.title: Continual improvement
requirements.purpose: Requires the organisation to keep making the system more suitable, adequate and effective.
requirements.guidance: Collect improvement ideas from audits, incidents, metrics, staff and customers, then record, prioritise and deliver them. A simple improvement log reviewed in management review is fine. Auditors want to see real changes made, not only a statement.
questions: Give examples of improvements you have made recently.
Where do ideas come from and how are they tracked?
How do you measure their effect?
Who prioritises?

requirements.title: Nonconformity and corrective action
requirements.purpose: Ensures problems are contained, their causes found and fixed so they do not come back.
requirements.guidance: When something fails or an audit finds a gap, react immediately to contain it, find the root cause, decide whether similar issues exist elsewhere, implement a fix and check it worked. If the cause shows that the risk assessment, a procedure or the system itself was wrong, update that too. Record everything in a log with owners and dates. Weak root cause analysis and actions that only address the symptom are the usual findings.
questions: How are nonconformities recorded and who manages them?
Show me one with root cause and the fix.
How do you check that corrective actions are effective?
Do you look for similar problems elsewhere?
evidence: Risk register or procedure updates made as a result of corrective action

requirements.title: A.5 · Organisational controls
requirements.purpose: Policies, roles, asset and access rules, suppliers, incidents, continuity and compliance: the management-level controls of Annex A.

requirements.title: Policies for information security
requirements.purpose: Gives staff and partners clear, approved rules for how information is protected.
requirements.guidance: Under the top-level policy from clause 5.2, keep topic-specific policies where your risks call for them, such as access control, acceptable use, backup, cryptography, supplier security and secure development. Each should have an owner, be approved at the right level of management, stay consistent with the top-level policy, and be reviewed on a set cycle and after significant change such as a new law, a major incident or a reorganisation. Make sure the people each policy applies to have received and acknowledged it. Write in plain language and avoid rules nobody follows. Auditors find topic policies that contradict each other, are out of date or were never communicated.
questions: Which topic-specific policies do you have, and how did your risks shape that list?
Who approves each topic policy and at what level of management?
What triggered the last review outside the normal cycle?
How do you check that topic policies do not conflict with the top-level policy or with each other?
How do you know the people each policy applies to have acknowledged it?
evidence: Policy set with owners, versions and approval
Mapping of topic policies to the risks or controls they support
Review log including reviews after significant change

requirements.title: Information security roles and responsibilities
requirements.purpose: Makes sure responsibility for protecting specific assets and running specific security activities is assigned to named people.
requirements.guidance: Clause 5.3 covers who runs and reports on the management system; this control goes further down. Assign owners for information assets, risks and controls, and responsibilities for activities such as access approval, backup checks, vulnerability handling and supplier reviews. Align the roles with your topic policies, and make sure each holder has the competence and time to do the job. Record responsibilities in role descriptions or owner fields in your registers, and tell people when they are given a duty. Auditors pick an asset or a control and ask its owner what they do and how often.
questions: Who owns this asset, risk or control, and what do they actually do?
How are people told when a security duty is given to them?
How do you check that role holders have the skills and time for their duties?
Show me where asset, risk and control owners are recorded.
evidence: Owner fields in asset, risk and control registers
Role descriptions with specific security duties
Notifications or acceptance of assigned duties

requirements.title: Segregation of duties
requirements.purpose: Reduces the chance of fraud or serious error by splitting tasks that should not be done by one person.
requirements.guidance: Identify high-risk combinations, for example requesting and approving access, writing and deploying code to production, or creating and approving payments. Split them between people or add independent review. Where the team is too small, use compensating measures such as logging and managerial review. Auditors look for admins who approve their own access.
questions: Which duties have you decided must be separated?
What do you do where a small team cannot separate them?
How is it enforced in tools?
Show me an example of an approval by a second person.
evidence: Workflow approvals in ticketing or code platform

requirements.title: Management responsibilities
requirements.purpose: Ensures managers actively require their teams to follow the security rules.
requirements.guidance: Managers should brief new team members before they get access, check compliance in day-to-day work, make time and tools available so the rules can be followed, and remind people of a confidential route for raising concerns. Build it into onboarding, performance conversations and team meetings. Breaches go through the disciplinary process in A.6.4; the manager's job is to spot problems early and support people. Auditors ask line managers what they do, not only the security lead.
questions: How do managers make sure their team follows the policies?
How do managers make time and resources available for security tasks in their team?
How are managers trained on their security duties?
Show me an example of a manager follow-up.
evidence: Confidential reporting route communicated to teams

requirements.title: Contact with authorities
requirements.purpose: Makes sure you can quickly reach the right authorities when security or legal matters arise.
requirements.guidance: Keep a list of the regulators, police, data protection authority, national CERT and emergency services relevant to you, with who is allowed to contact them and when. Include the reporting deadlines you know apply. Test that the contacts are current. A list nobody has looked at in two years is the usual weakness.
questions: Which authorities might you need to contact and who decides?
Where are contact details kept?
When was the list last checked?
How does this link to your incident process?

requirements.title: Contact with special interest groups
requirements.purpose: Keeps the organisation informed through professional communities and security forums.
requirements.guidance: Join relevant groups, mailing lists, vendor advisories or industry bodies, and make someone responsible for reading and passing on important items. Record what you learn and what you changed. It does not need to be costly; free advisories and local meetups count if used.
questions: Which groups or forums do you follow?
Who monitors them?
Give an example of something learned that changed your practice.
How is the membership reviewed?

requirements.title: Threat intelligence
requirements.purpose: Turns information about current threats into decisions about your defences.
requirements.guidance: Collect threat information from sources fitting your sector, such as vendor bulletins, national CERT alerts and industry sharing groups. Analyse what is relevant and feed it into risk assessment, patching priorities and detection. Keep it proportionate; a monthly review of a few trusted feeds is acceptable for a small company.
questions: Where do you get threat information?
Who analyses it and how often?
Show a case where it changed a priority or control.
How is it shared internally?

requirements.title: Information security in project management
requirements.purpose: Builds security into projects from the start rather than adding it at the end.
requirements.guidance: Add a simple security step to the project template: identify information involved, assess risk, set requirements and check before go-live. Apply it to internal changes and customer deliveries. Auditors sample projects and look for evidence the step was done.
questions: How is security considered when a project begins?
Show me a recent project's security assessment.
Who signs off before go-live?
How are risks tracked during the project?

requirements.title: Inventory of information and other associated assets
requirements.purpose: Gives you a complete picture of what needs protecting and who is responsible.
requirements.guidance: Maintain a register of information assets, systems, services, devices and key data stores, each with an owner and a classification. Pull from tooling where possible to keep it current, and review it regularly. Common failings are shadow IT missing from the list and assets without owners.
questions: Where is your asset inventory and how is it kept current?
Who are the owners?
How do you discover unknown assets?
Does the inventory cover cloud services and data?
evidence: Asset register with owners and classification

requirements.title: Acceptable use of information and other associated assets
requirements.purpose: Sets clear rules for how staff may handle information and equipment.
requirements.guidance: Write an acceptable use rule covering devices, email, internet, personal use, removable media, software and handling of customer data. Staff should acknowledge it on joining and when it changes. Keep it brief enough to be read. Auditors ask staff what they may and may not do.
questions: Where are the rules for acceptable use?
How do new starters accept them?
How do you handle breaches?
Does it cover personal devices and remote work?

requirements.title: Return of assets
requirements.purpose: Makes sure equipment and information come back when people leave or change role.
requirements.guidance: Use a leaver checklist covering laptops, phones, tokens, keys, documents and data, and tie it to HR so no leaver slips through. Collect, wipe and record. Auditors compare the leaver list from HR with returns records.
questions: How do you recover assets from leavers?
How do you know nothing was missed?
What happens to data on personal devices?
Show me a recent leaver's record.
evidence: HR leaver list matched to returns

requirements.title: Classification of information
requirements.purpose: Lets you apply the right level of protection by grouping information according to its sensitivity.
requirements.guidance: Define a small number of classes, typically three or four, with criteria and examples, and an owner who assigns them. Base the scheme on confidentiality, integrity and availability needs plus legal duties. Simple beats elaborate. Auditors find schemes nobody applies.
questions: What classes do you use and how are they defined?
Who decides the class of a dataset?
Show examples of classified items.
How is the scheme reviewed?

requirements.title: Labelling of information
requirements.purpose: Helps people recognise how sensitive an item is so they handle it correctly.
requirements.guidance: Decide how each class is marked in documents, emails, systems and storage, and what handling rules follow. Use templates, headers and tool features to make labelling automatic where possible. Give staff short guidance. Check labels in sampled documents.
questions: How do you label information?
What handling follows each label?
Is labelling automated?
Show me examples.

requirements.title: Information transfer
requirements.purpose: Protects information when it is sent, shared or moved between parties.
requirements.guidance: Set rules per channel, such as email, file sharing, courier, messaging and APIs, covering approved tools, encryption and who may send what. For external parties include agreements on handling. Check what actually happens, for instance whether staff use personal webmail.
questions: Which channels are approved for which classes?
How is encryption applied?
What agreements cover transfers to third parties?
Show me an example of a secure transfer.

requirements.title: Access control
requirements.purpose: Ensures access to information and systems is granted on the basis of need and policy.
requirements.guidance: Document an access rule built on need to know and least privilege, covering business and security requirements for each system. Apply it consistently across applications, networks and physical areas. Auditors test whether real access matches the rule.
questions: What is your access control rule?
How is it applied across systems?
Who owns approval for each system?
Show me how you tested it.

requirements.title: Identity management
requirements.purpose: Controls the full lifecycle of user and system identities.
requirements.guidance: Give every person and service account a unique identity, approve creation, record the owner, and remove it when no longer needed. Avoid shared accounts or document the exceptions. Link it to HR joiner, mover and leaver steps. Common gaps are orphaned accounts of former staff.
questions: How are identities created and removed?
How do you handle shared or service accounts?
How do you find orphaned accounts?
Who is responsible?

requirements.title: Authentication information
requirements.purpose: Protects passwords, keys and other secrets throughout their life.
requirements.guidance: Control how passwords, PINs, keys, tokens and other secrets are issued, used and changed. Issue initial secrets through a secure channel and force a change at first use, set a sensible standard for password quality, provide a password manager, and tell people not to share or reuse credentials. Machine secrets such as API keys belong in a vault, not in code or documents, and are rotated on a schedule and at once after suspected exposure. How strong the sign-in itself is, including multi-factor authentication, is covered by A.8.5. Auditors look for secrets in repositories, shared spreadsheets of passwords and default credentials left unchanged.
questions: How are initial passwords and tokens issued and changed at first use?
What guidance do staff receive on handling their credentials?
How are API keys and other machine secrets stored and rotated?
What happens when a credential may have been exposed?
evidence: Authentication information standard or password guideline
Secret vault inventory and rotation logs
Secret scanning reports from code repositories
Records of credential resets after suspected exposure

requirements.title: Access rights
requirements.purpose: Ensures permissions are properly granted, reviewed and removed.
requirements.guidance: Use a request and approval flow for access, give roles that match jobs, and run periodic reviews of who can reach critical systems, with action on exceptions. Remove rights on role changes and leaving. Auditors pick users and verify the approval trail.
questions: How are access rights requested and approved?
How often are they reviewed?
Show me the last review and what was removed.
How quickly are leavers removed?
evidence: Mover records showing rights adjusted on role change

requirements.title: Information security in supplier relationships
requirements.purpose: Manages the risk that comes with suppliers who touch your information or services.
requirements.guidance: Keep a supplier register, rate each by the data and criticality involved, and set security expectations by tier. Do a proportionate check before onboarding: questionnaire, certificate or report review. Auditors look for critical suppliers with no assessment.
questions: Which suppliers are most critical to you?
How do you assess them before engagement?
How are risks tracked?
Who owns the relationship?

requirements.title: Addressing information security within supplier agreements
requirements.purpose: Puts security expectations into contracts so they are enforceable.
requirements.guidance: Include clauses on confidentiality, data handling, incident notification, audit or evidence rights, subcontractors and exit. Use a standard addendum for common cases. Check that signed contracts exist for key suppliers. Missing breach notification terms are a typical gap.
questions: What security terms do your supplier contracts include?
Do you have them for all critical suppliers?
How do you handle subcontractors?
What happens at exit?

requirements.title: Managing information security in the ICT supply chain
requirements.purpose: Addresses risk from the chain of technology products and services your own suppliers depend on.
requirements.guidance: Ask key ICT suppliers how they manage their own suppliers, ask for provenance and update commitments, and avoid single points of failure. Capture requirements for software components and cloud services. Keep it proportionate to your reliance.
questions: How do you understand your suppliers' suppliers?
What do you require of ICT providers?
How do you manage open-source components?
Which dependencies are single points of failure?

requirements.title: Monitoring, review and change management of supplier services
requirements.purpose: Keeps supplier performance and security under review through the life of the relationship.
requirements.guidance: Review critical suppliers at least yearly: service reports, incidents, certificates, financial or security changes. Record outcomes and actions, and handle supplier changes through a controlled process. Auditors expect records of reviews, not only the initial check.
questions: How often do you review suppliers?
What do you do when a supplier's circumstances change?
Show me a review record.
How are supplier incidents tracked?

requirements.title: Information security for use of cloud services
requirements.purpose: Sets how cloud services are chosen, configured, used and exited.
requirements.guidance: Define criteria for selecting providers, the shared responsibility split, configuration baselines and exit plans. Keep a list of all cloud services and their owners. Review settings regularly. Auditors find unapproved services and default configurations.
questions: How are cloud services approved?
Who is responsible for configuration?
How is data protected there?
What is your exit plan?

requirements.title: Information security incident management planning and preparation
requirements.purpose: Prepares roles, processes and tools so incidents are handled quickly and consistently.
requirements.guidance: Write an incident procedure naming roles, severity levels, contact paths and decision rights, and make sure people know how to report. Prepare tooling and templates in advance. Test it with an exercise. Plans that live only in the security lead's head are a common finding.
questions: Who is in the incident team and what are their roles?
How do staff report incidents?
When did you last test the process?
Where are contacts and templates?

requirements.title: Assessment and decision on information security events
requirements.purpose: Makes sure reported events are triaged and classified consistently.
requirements.guidance: Use defined criteria to decide if an event is an incident and how severe, and record the decision. Keep a log of all reported events, even those dismissed. Auditors compare log entries with the criteria.
questions: How do you decide if an event is an incident?
Who makes the call?
Show me a dismissed event and why.
How do you rate severity?

requirements.title: Response to information security incidents
requirements.purpose: Ensures incidents are contained, resolved and communicated in an orderly way.
requirements.guidance: Follow documented steps: contain, investigate, eradicate, recover, and notify those entitled to know, including regulators and customers within legal timelines. Keep timestamps and decisions. Auditors review a real incident file.
questions: Walk me through your last incident.
How did you decide who to notify?
How quickly did you respond?
What records were kept?

requirements.title: Learning from information security incidents
requirements.purpose: Uses incidents to improve controls and prevent repeats.
requirements.guidance: After each significant incident or near miss, hold a short review, record root cause and agree actions that are tracked to close. Share lessons with staff. Review trends of incidents periodically.
questions: What did you learn from your last incident?
Which controls changed as a result?
How are actions tracked?
Do you look at trends?

requirements.title: Collection of evidence
requirements.purpose: Preserves information that may be needed for investigation, legal or disciplinary action.
requirements.guidance: Define how logs, devices and other evidence are identified, collected and kept so their integrity holds up, with a chain of custody. Know when to call forensic help. Keep it simple for small organisations, but agree in advance how you would obtain evidence held by cloud providers and other suppliers, and consider whether it needs to stand up in court in each country involved.
questions: How do you preserve evidence in an incident?
Who is authorised to collect it?
How do you protect its integrity?
How would you obtain and preserve evidence held by a cloud provider or another supplier?
evidence: Supplier or cloud terms covering access to evidence

requirements.title: Information security during disruption
requirements.purpose: Keeps security in place when normal operations are interrupted.
requirements.guidance: Identify which controls must continue during a disaster or crisis, and plan for alternative measures such as manual access approval or secure remote working. Include these in continuity plans. Test them. Auditors want to see security considered in continuity exercises.
questions: Which security controls must continue in a disruption?
What alternatives have you planned?
Have you tested them?
Who decides on temporary exceptions?

requirements.title: ICT readiness for business continuity
requirements.purpose: Makes sure technology can be recovered to meet business needs.
requirements.guidance: Set recovery time and recovery point targets for each critical service from a business impact analysis, and get the business owners to agree them. Then design the technical side to meet them: redundancy, failover, alternative sites or cloud regions, and documented ICT continuity plans that recover systems in the right order with their dependencies. Test the plans through failover or recovery exercises and compare the results with the targets. Backups themselves are covered by A.8.13; here the question is whether whole services come back in time. Common findings are targets nobody agreed and continuity plans never exercised.
questions: What are your recovery targets and who agreed them?
How does your technical design meet those targets?
When did you last exercise recovery of a whole service and what did it show?
How are dependencies on suppliers and other systems built into the recovery order?
evidence: Agreed recovery time and recovery point targets
ICT continuity plans and recovery runbooks
Failover or recovery exercise reports compared with targets

requirements.title: Legal, statutory, regulatory and contractual requirements
requirements.purpose: Ensures you know and meet the laws and contracts that affect information security.
requirements.guidance: Keep a register of applicable laws, regulations and key customer obligations, with an owner and how each is met. Review it at least yearly or when you enter a new market. Seek legal advice where unsure. Auditors check that data protection and customer terms are in it.
questions: Which laws and contracts affect you?
Who maintains the register?
How do you learn about changes?
How do you show compliance?

requirements.title: Intellectual property rights
requirements.purpose: Prevents infringement of licences and protects your own IP.
requirements.guidance: Keep track of software licences, use approved sources, restrict unauthorised installation and check use against what was bought. Record ownership of what you create and use. Auditors sample devices for unlicensed software.
questions: How do you track licences?
How do you prevent unlicensed software?
How do you protect your own IP?
How is open-source use controlled?

requirements.title: Protection of records
requirements.purpose: Keeps the records you rely on for legal, contractual and business reasons intact, available and confidential for as long as they are needed.
requirements.guidance: Identify record types, assign retention periods based on law and business need, store them securely and dispose of them properly at the end. Protect integrity, for example with access limits and backups. Auditors ask about retention and deletion in practice.
questions: What records do you keep and for how long?
How are they protected from change?
How are they destroyed?
Who owns the retention schedule?

requirements.title: Privacy and protection of PII
requirements.purpose: Makes sure personal data is handled in line with privacy law and obligations.
requirements.guidance: Know what personal data you hold, why, where and for how long, assign privacy responsibilities, and have processes for individual requests and breaches. Align with GDPR or your applicable law. Keep records of processing and supplier agreements.
questions: What personal data do you process and where?
Who is responsible for privacy?
How do you handle subject requests?
What is your breach notification process?

requirements.title: Independent review of information security
requirements.purpose: Gives management an independent view of whether the way security is managed, and how it is put into practice, is still right.
requirements.guidance: Arrange reviews at planned intervals and after significant change, carried out by people who do not work in the area being reviewed: an internal audit function, a manager from another part of the business or an outside specialist. Look at the overall approach, people, processes and technology, not only rule compliance. An independent internal audit can meet this control if it covers that ground; most certification bodies will not accept their own audit as the review. Report the results to management and track the actions that follow.
questions: Who carried out the last independent review and how was their independence assured?
What triggered it: the schedule or a significant change?
Did it look at the overall approach as well as compliance, and what did it find?
How were the results reported and acted on?

requirements.title: Compliance with policies, rules and standards for information security
requirements.purpose: Checks that people and systems follow the rules you set.
requirements.guidance: Managers and system owners should periodically verify their areas, using automated checks where possible, such as configuration compliance. Record deviations and fix them. Report results to the system owner.
questions: How do you check compliance with policies?
Who performs the checks?
What do you do with deviations?
Show me results from the last check.

requirements.title: Documented operating procedures
requirements.purpose: Ensures routine operations are done consistently and can be performed by others.
requirements.guidance: Write short procedures for tasks such as backup, onboarding, deployment and monitoring, make them available to those who need them, and update them when processes change. Keep them practical. Auditors ask operators whether the procedure matches what they do.
questions: Which operating procedures exist?
Who maintains them?
Are they accessible to operators?
How are changes reflected?

requirements.title: A.6 · People controls
requirements.purpose: Covers how the organisation manages security across the working life of its people, from hiring to leaving, including awareness, remote work and reporting problems.

requirements.title: Screening
requirements.purpose: Reduce the risk of hiring or engaging someone unsuitable by checking people before they get access to your information and again when their role or risk changes.
requirements.guidance: Decide which roles need which checks, based on the access and sensitivity involved, and write it down so it is applied consistently. Typical checks are identity, right to work, references and qualifications, with criminal record or credit checks only where local law allows and the role justifies it. Apply the same rules to contractors and agency staff, either directly or by requiring the agency or supplier to carry them out and confirm the result. Screening is not a one-off: repeat or extend checks when someone moves into a more sensitive role and, for high-trust roles, at an interval you define. Decide in advance what happens if a check is not finished by the start date, such as starting with restricted access. Auditors often find checks done for some hires but not others, or no record that they were completed before the start date.
questions: How do you decide which checks apply to which roles, and where is that recorded?
Can you show the checks completed for the last few joiners before their first day?
How are contractors and agency staff screened, and how does the supplier confirm it?
When are checks repeated, for example when someone moves into a more sensitive role?
What happens if a check is unfinished at the start date or returns a concern?
evidence: Screening procedure listing checks by role
Completed check records or HR checklist for recent joiners
Signed consent forms for checks where required
Agency or supplier confirmations of contractor screening
Re-screening records for people moved into sensitive roles

requirements.title: Terms and conditions of employment
requirements.purpose: Make sure people know from the start what security responsibilities they carry and agree to them in writing.
requirements.guidance: Include a short security clause in employment contracts and contractor agreements that points to the key policies and states that people must follow them. Make clear that responsibilities apply to information handled for the organisation and to company property. Keep signed copies and make sure changes to the policies are communicated rather than silently updated. A common gap is contractors or interns who started without signing anything.
questions: Where in the contract are security responsibilities set out?
How do new joiners confirm they have read the policies?
Do contractors and temporary staff sign equivalent terms?
How are people told when the terms or policies change?
evidence: Contract template with information security clause
Signed contracts or acknowledgements for a sample of staff
Contractor agreement template with security terms

requirements.title: Information security awareness, education and training
requirements.purpose: Give people the knowledge to behave securely in their daily work and to know what is expected of them.
requirements.guidance: Give every joiner a security induction before or soon after they get access, and refresh everyone at an interval you set, commonly yearly, and whenever a policy that affects them changes materially. Cover the policies that apply to them, phishing and social engineering, safe handling of data and how to report a problem. Add role-specific training for people with extra risk, such as administrators, developers or finance staff, and include contractors and other external people who work with your information. Track completion and check understanding with a short quiz or a simulated phishing exercise, then use the results and real incidents to update the content. Auditors look for evidence that everyone was trained, including late joiners, part-timers and contractors, and that people were told when a policy changed.
questions: How are new joiners and contractors trained, and how soon after they get access?
How do you know everyone completed the latest refresher?
What extra training do privileged or high-risk roles get?
How are people told about changes to policies that affect them?
How do you measure whether awareness is working, and what did you change as a result?
evidence: Training plan and content for the year
Completion records for staff and contractors
Phishing simulation results and follow-up actions
Role-specific training records for administrators and developers

requirements.title: Disciplinary process
requirements.purpose: Have a fair, known way to respond when someone breaks security rules, so the rules carry weight.
requirements.guidance: Use your existing HR disciplinary procedure and make sure it explicitly covers breaches of information security policy; reach contractors and suppliers through terms in their contracts. Staff should know the process exists, for example through the handbook or induction. Establish the facts before any action, usually through the incident or HR investigation, so nobody is sanctioned on suspicion alone. Keep responses proportionate to what actually happened, so an honest slip by someone never shown the rules is handled differently from deliberate misuse. Involve HR and legal advice so employment law is respected. Auditors usually ask whether the process has been used and whether lessons from cases feed back into training.
questions: Does the disciplinary procedure cover security breaches explicitly, and how does it reach contractors?
How are staff made aware of the consequences?
How do you confirm that a breach happened before the process starts?
Has the process been used, and how was proportionality decided?
How are lessons from cases fed back into training or controls?
evidence: Staff handbook section or induction slide on consequences
Contractor agreement clause on security breaches
Anonymised case file showing investigation and outcome
Acknowledgement of the policy by staff

requirements.title: Responsibilities after termination or change of employment
requirements.purpose: Make sure people who leave or change role know which security duties stay with them afterwards, and that those duties are enforced.
requirements.guidance: Decide which duties carry on after someone leaves or moves, such as confidentiality, protection of intellectual property and any restrictions agreed in the contract, and write them into contracts and confidentiality agreements. Remind people of these duties at the exit meeting or in a leaver letter and get an acknowledgement where possible. When someone changes role, hand the security responsibilities of the old role to a named successor and confirm which new duties apply. Trigger the process from HR events so it does not rely on memory. Return of assets (A.5.11) and removal of access (A.5.18) usually run from the same leaver and mover checklist, so link to them rather than repeating them here. Auditors look for leavers who were never reminded of continuing duties and security roles left empty after a move.
questions: Which security duties continue after employment ends, and where are they written down?
How are leavers reminded of those duties, and how is that recorded?
When someone changes role, how are their security responsibilities handed over?
How is the leaver and mover process triggered from HR events?
What would you do if a former employee or contractor breached a continuing duty?
evidence: Contract and confidentiality clauses on duties that survive termination
Leaver letter or signed exit acknowledgement
Completed leaver and mover checklists for a recent sample
Handover records for people who held security roles
HR leaver and mover notifications with dates

requirements.title: Confidentiality or non-disclosure agreements
requirements.purpose: Protect sensitive information by getting a clear, signed commitment to confidentiality from anyone who may see it.
requirements.guidance: Use standard agreements for staff, contractors, suppliers and visitors who may see sensitive material, and take legal advice on the wording. Make each agreement say plainly which information it protects, how long the obligation runs (often beyond the end of the relationship), what must happen to the information at the end and what follows a breach. Identify the situations that need an agreement, such as supplier onboarding, partner discussions or due diligence, so it is signed before access rather than after. Review the templates at planned intervals and when your business or the law changes. Auditors check that agreements are signed before access is granted and that you can find them easily.
questions: Who is asked to sign confidentiality agreements, and at what point?
How do you decide which relationships need an agreement?
When were the templates last reviewed, and what triggers a review?
How do you confirm agreements are signed before access starts?
How are signed agreements stored and found again?
evidence: Current agreement templates with review date
Signed agreements for a sample of staff and suppliers
Register of agreements with expiry or review dates
Supplier onboarding checklist showing agreement step

requirements.title: Remote working
requirements.purpose: Keep information safe when people work from home, on the move or at client sites.
requirements.guidance: Set simple rules for remote work: approved devices, a protected connection such as a VPN or zero-trust access, screen locking, private space and no use of public Wi-Fi for sensitive work without protection. Cover paper, printing and calls that can be overheard. Make sure remote staff get the same training and support as office staff. Auditors often find policy and practice differ, such as personal devices used with no controls.
questions: What is your policy for working from home or while travelling?
How are remote devices protected and managed?
How do staff connect to company systems from outside?
How do you handle printing or paper at home?
evidence: VPN or secure access configuration evidence
Awareness material on remote working risks

requirements.title: Information security event reporting
requirements.purpose: Make sure problems are spotted and reported quickly so they can be handled before they grow.
requirements.guidance: Give people one clear, easy way to report anything suspicious, such as a dedicated mailbox, chat channel or form, and make it known in induction and training. Explain what to report, including near misses, lost devices and odd emails, and make clear nobody is punished for good-faith reports. Log every report and triage it. Auditors look for evidence that staff actually use the channel and that reports are followed up.
questions: How do staff report a suspected security problem?
How do you encourage reporting of near misses?
Can you show reports received and what happened to them?
How quickly are reports acknowledged and triaged?
evidence: Log of reported events with outcomes
Awareness material explaining how to report

requirements.title: A.7 · Physical controls
requirements.purpose: Covers protecting buildings, rooms, equipment and media from unauthorised entry, damage and loss.

requirements.title: Physical security perimeters
requirements.purpose: Define and protect the boundaries around areas that hold information or systems.
requirements.guidance: Identify which areas need protection, such as offices, server rooms and storage, and mark their boundaries with real barriers like locked doors, walls and entry control. Match the strength of protection to the sensitivity of what is inside. Check boundaries have no weak points such as propped doors or unlocked windows. For shared buildings, agree with the landlord who controls what.
questions: Which areas hold sensitive information or equipment?
How are the boundaries of these areas protected?
How do you check doors and windows are secure?
What is your arrangement with the landlord for shared buildings?
evidence: Photos or inspection record of doors and locks

requirements.title: Physical entry
requirements.purpose: Make sure only authorised people can enter your premises and secure areas.
requirements.guidance: Use badges, keys, codes or reception checks to control entry, and keep records of who holds access. Sign in visitors, issue visitor passes, and escort them in sensitive areas. Treat delivery, loading and post areas as entry points too: keep them apart from secure areas where you can, inspect incoming items, and stop couriers and drivers from walking into the building unescorted. Remove access promptly when people leave and review who has access to critical rooms regularly. Auditors typically find old badges still active, shared door codes and visitor logs that are incomplete.
questions: How do you control who enters the building and sensitive rooms?
How are visitors recorded and escorted?
How are deliveries and couriers handled so they do not give a way into secure areas?
How often is access to secure areas reviewed?
What happens to badges, keys and codes when someone leaves?
evidence: Access control system list of badge holders
Access review record for secure areas

requirements.title: Securing offices, rooms and facilities
requirements.purpose: Prevent unauthorised people from seeing or reaching information through the way rooms and buildings are set up.
requirements.guidance: Choose locations for sensitive work and equipment that are not visible or easily reached from public areas. Keep server and comms rooms locked and unmarked, and avoid signs that advertise where valuable assets are kept. Position screens, printers and meeting rooms so confidential material cannot be seen or overheard. Review the layout when you move or refit.
questions: Which rooms hold sensitive equipment or discussions?
How are they protected from view and access?
Can visitors see screens or documents from public areas?
Is there signage that reveals where valuable assets are?
evidence: Floor plan with secure rooms marked
Photos of locked comms or server rooms
Key or access list for sensitive rooms

requirements.title: Physical security monitoring
requirements.purpose: Detect unauthorised physical access or suspicious activity so it can be acted on.
requirements.guidance: Use means proportionate to your site, such as alarms, CCTV, security staff or building management services, and make sure someone responds to alerts. Test alarms regularly and keep recordings only as long as needed, respecting privacy rules and telling people they are filmed. Check the monitoring covers entrances and sensitive rooms. Typical gaps are cameras not recording and nobody reviewing alerts.
questions: How do you detect unauthorised entry outside working hours?
Who responds when an alarm goes off?
How long are recordings kept and who can view them?
When were alarms and cameras last tested?
evidence: Incident log of physical alerts and responses

requirements.title: Protecting against physical and environmental threats
requirements.purpose: Reduce damage from fire, flood, heat, theft and other physical hazards.
requirements.guidance: Assess the hazards that apply to your location, such as flooding, fire, extreme weather or neighbouring risks, and put sensible protections in place. Typical measures are smoke detection, extinguishers, water sensors, safe storage of backups and keeping critical equipment out of risky spots. Link this to business continuity so you know what happens if a site is lost. Auditors want to see the assessment and proof of tested equipment.
questions: Which physical and environmental hazards apply to your sites?
What protections are in place for key equipment?
When were fire and other safety systems last tested?
How does this link to your continuity plans?
evidence: Fire safety inspection and extinguisher servicing records
Environmental sensor or detector test logs
Continuity plan covering loss of site

requirements.title: Working in secure areas
requirements.purpose: Set behaviour rules for people who work inside areas that need extra protection.
requirements.guidance: Write down the house rules for each secure area, for example that visitors and contractors are always accompanied, that cameras and recording devices need permission and that the room is locked and checked when nobody is using it. Share details of what a secure area holds and how it is protected only with the people whose work requires it. Post the rules at the entrance and include them in the briefing for anyone given access. Check that unused secure rooms are locked and as expected during routine walk-rounds.
questions: What rules apply inside your secure areas?
How are staff and contractors told about these rules?
How are empty secure rooms checked and locked?
Are cameras and personal devices restricted?
evidence: Induction record for people with access

requirements.title: Clear desk and clear screen
requirements.purpose: Stop information being seen or taken because it was left on desks, printers or open screens.
requirements.guidance: Set a simple rule that papers and removable media are put away and screens are locked when you leave your seat, enforced by an automatic screen lock after a short idle time. Provide lockable storage and secure shredding. Check printers and meeting rooms for forgotten documents. Auditors often do a walk-around and note unlocked screens or papers left out, so spot checks pay off.
questions: What is your rule for desks and screens?
Is automatic screen lock enforced and how?
How do you check compliance in the office?
How is confidential paper stored and destroyed?
evidence: Shredding bins or secure disposal records

requirements.title: Equipment siting and protection
requirements.purpose: Place and protect equipment so it is safe from damage, theft and prying eyes.
requirements.guidance: Put servers, network gear and sensitive displays in locations that reduce risk from water, power surges, theft and unauthorised viewing. Use racks, cabinets and cable locks where appropriate, and keep food and drink away from critical kit. For cloud-based businesses this mostly concerns office networking, printers and staff devices. Review where equipment sits whenever the office layout changes.
questions: Where is critical equipment kept and why there?
How is it protected from theft, damage and being seen?
Are any devices in public or shared areas?
How do you keep an equipment location record?
evidence: Equipment location list or asset register entries
