Photos of comms cabinets and racks

requirements.title: Security of assets off-premises
requirements.purpose: Keep equipment and information safe when it leaves your building.
requirements.guidance: Set rules for taking laptops, phones and papers away, such as never leaving them unattended in vehicles, using encryption and screen privacy filters when travelling. Record who holds which asset and require reporting of loss straight away. Provide guidance for travel to higher-risk countries. Auditors check that off-site devices are encrypted and tracked.
questions: What rules apply to taking equipment off site?
How are devices protected when travelling?
How do staff report lost or stolen equipment?
How do you track which assets are off site?

requirements.title: Storage media
requirements.purpose: Control USB drives, external disks, memory cards and other removable media throughout their life so the information on them is not lost or exposed.
requirements.guidance: Decide whether removable media is allowed at all, and if so restrict it to approved encrypted devices. Handle each item according to the classification of the data on it, from issue through use, transport and storage to final destruction. Keep an inventory of media in use, store it securely and track movement when it is sent elsewhere, using trusted couriers and tamper-evident packaging for sensitive items. Define how media is wiped or destroyed when no longer needed, and keep a record. Many small firms reduce risk by blocking USB storage on laptops and using managed cloud sharing instead.
questions: Is removable media allowed and under what conditions?
How does the classification of the data change how media is handled?
How is media protected and tracked when it is sent or carried elsewhere?
How do you stop unapproved USB use?
How is media wiped or destroyed at the end of life?
evidence: Endpoint configuration blocking or controlling USB

requirements.title: Supporting utilities
requirements.purpose: Keep power, cooling, connectivity and similar services reliable so systems are not lost to utility failures.
requirements.guidance: Identify the utilities your critical systems depend on and consider the impact of an outage. Provide protection that fits the risk, such as battery backup for key equipment, surge protection and a second internet connection. Test backup power where installed and agree support terms with providers. If services are in the cloud, rely on provider assurance but cover your own office dependencies.
questions: Which utilities do your critical services depend on?
What happens if power or internet fails?
When was backup power last tested?
What assurance do you hold that hosting providers protect their own power, cooling and connectivity?
evidence: Continuity plan section for utility failure

requirements.title: Cabling security
requirements.purpose: Protect network and power cables from interception, interference and damage.
requirements.guidance: Keep network and power cabling tidy, labelled and out of public reach, with comms cupboards locked. Separate power and data cabling where interference is a risk. Consider conduit or locked trunking where cables pass through shared spaces. Check sockets in meeting rooms and reception are disabled or controlled so visitors cannot plug in.
questions: How are network cables protected from tampering?
Can a visitor plug into your network from a public area?
Are comms cabinets locked?
How is cabling documented?
evidence: Photos of cabling and comms cabinets

requirements.title: Equipment maintenance
requirements.purpose: Keep equipment working and safe through regular, controlled maintenance.
requirements.guidance: Follow supplier recommendations for servicing and keep records of repairs and faults. Make sure only authorised people carry out maintenance, and remove or protect data before equipment goes for repair. Supervise third-party engineers on site. Include firmware and hardware updates in the schedule so devices are not left unsupported.
questions: How do you schedule maintenance for key equipment?
Who is allowed to repair or service it?
How is data protected when equipment is sent for repair?
How do you track warranties and support ends?

requirements.title: Secure disposal or re-use of equipment
requirements.purpose: Make sure no information remains on equipment you throw away, sell or hand to someone else.
requirements.guidance: Before disposal or reuse, wipe storage using a recognised method or physically destroy it, and keep a record of what was done to each item. Remove or reassign licensed software as well as data, and check every device that can hold information, including printers, copiers, phones, network equipment and old servers. For damaged devices, decide whether destruction is safer than sending them out for repair. Use a trustworthy disposal provider and get certificates that list serial numbers. Auditors often find retired laptops in cupboards with data still on them.
questions: How do you remove data from equipment before disposal or reuse?
Who does the wiping and how is it verified?
How is licensed software removed or reassigned from retired devices?
Do you use a disposal provider and get certificates?
How do you account for retired and damaged devices?
evidence: Data wipe or destruction certificates listing serial numbers
Software licence register updated for retired devices

requirements.title: A.8 · Technological controls
requirements.purpose: Covers the technical safeguards for devices, access, data, networks, software and development that keep information secure in day-to-day operations.

requirements.title: User endpoint devices
requirements.purpose: Keep laptops, phones and other devices used for work secure wherever they are.
requirements.guidance: Set a baseline for all devices that connect to company data, including encryption, passcodes, automatic locking, up-to-date software and the ability to wipe remotely. Use device management tools where possible to enforce this. Decide what is allowed on personal devices and apply the same standards. Auditors typically sample devices and find missing encryption or out-of-date operating systems.
questions: What security settings are required on every device?
How do you check that devices comply?
What is the rule for personal devices?
How do you wipe a lost device?

requirements.title: Privileged access rights
requirements.purpose: Limit and control powerful accounts because misuse of them causes the greatest damage.
requirements.guidance: Keep a list of who has admin or elevated rights, grant them only where there is a real need and use separate admin accounts from everyday ones. Prefer time-limited or just-in-time elevation over standing rights, and avoid generic shared admin accounts. Require stronger sign-in for these accounts and review them at planned intervals, more often than ordinary access. Log what privileged users do and have someone other than the user check those logs. Typical findings are shared admin accounts, former staff keeping rights and no review.
questions: Who has administrative access and why?
How are privileged accounts requested and approved?
Which privileged access is granted only for a limited time?
How often are privileged rights reviewed, and by whom?
Are admin actions logged, and who checks them?
evidence: List of privileged accounts with owners

requirements.title: Information access restriction
requirements.purpose: Make sure people can only see and change information their job needs.
requirements.guidance: Define access by role, apply least privilege and set it up in each system, including shared drives and cloud apps. Review who can reach sensitive folders and customer data at planned intervals. Restrict external sharing links and guest access. Auditors check that the rules in policy match what systems actually allow.
questions: How is access to systems and data decided?
How do you stop people reaching information they do not need?
How often is access reviewed?
How is external sharing controlled?
evidence: Access control policy and role matrix
System permission exports for key systems

requirements.title: Access to source code
requirements.purpose: Protect code and the tools around it from unauthorised viewing and changes.
requirements.guidance: Restrict repository access by team and need, and give write access only to those who must change code. Apply the same thinking to build pipelines, development tools and package libraries, since control of those lets someone change what is shipped. Protect main branches so changes merge only through review. Use strong sign-in and log who reads and changes code. Keep code and libraries in controlled places, not on personal drives or unmanaged accounts.
questions: Who can read and who can change your repositories?
How is access to build pipelines, development tools and package libraries controlled?
How are protected branches set up so changes cannot skip review?
How is access removed when developers or contractors leave?
evidence: Build pipeline and package registry access settings

requirements.title: Secure authentication
requirements.purpose: Make sure people prove who they are in a way that is hard to fake.
requirements.guidance: Use unique accounts, strong or passwordless sign-in and multi-factor authentication for remote access, admin accounts and anything holding sensitive data. Block weak and reused passwords and lock out repeated failures. Use single sign-on where possible to reduce password sprawl. Auditors look for exceptions such as shared logins and services without multi-factor authentication.
questions: How do users authenticate to key systems?
Where is multi-factor authentication required?
How do you prevent weak passwords?
How are shared or service accounts handled?

requirements.title: Capacity management
requirements.purpose: Make sure systems have enough resources for current and future demand.
requirements.guidance: Monitor key resources like storage, memory, processing and bandwidth, and set alerts before they run out. Review trends and plan upgrades or scaling ahead of need. Consider seasonal peaks and growth, including cloud service limits and costs. Record decisions so capacity does not become a surprise outage.
questions: How do you monitor the capacity of critical systems?
What alerts warn you before limits are reached?
How do you forecast future needs?
Has a capacity shortfall caused an incident?

requirements.title: Protection against malware
requirements.purpose: Prevent, detect and clean up malicious software on your systems.
requirements.guidance: Install and update endpoint protection on all devices and servers, and scan email and downloads. Limit who can install software and block known bad sources. Teach people to spot suspicious links and attachments. Make sure detections are reviewed and someone acts on them. Auditors look for devices missing the agent or with outdated definitions.
questions: What malware protection is on devices and servers?
How are updates and coverage checked?
How are detections handled?
How are staff trained to avoid malware?

requirements.title: Management of technical vulnerabilities
requirements.purpose: Find and fix weaknesses in systems before attackers use them.
requirements.guidance: Keep an inventory of what you run, scan regularly and apply patches within times based on severity, for example critical fixes within days. Track exceptions with an approved reason and compensating measures. Subscribe to supplier and security advisories. Test patches where practical. Typical findings are unpatched servers and no record of how fast fixes are applied.
questions: How do you learn about vulnerabilities in your systems?
What are your patching timelines?
How do you track and close findings?
How are exceptions approved?

requirements.title: Configuration management
requirements.purpose: Keep systems set up securely and stop settings drifting unnoticed.
requirements.guidance: Define secure baseline settings for servers, devices, cloud services and network equipment, and apply them consistently, ideally through templates or infrastructure as code. Review configurations regularly and track changes. Remove default accounts and unneeded services. Auditors compare actual settings to the baseline and ask how drift is found.
questions: What baselines do you use for key systems?
How do you apply and check them?
How are changes to configurations tracked?
How do you handle default accounts and services?

requirements.title: Information deletion
requirements.purpose: Remove information when it is no longer needed so it cannot leak or be misused.
requirements.guidance: Set retention periods by type of data, based on legal, contract and business needs, and delete systematically when time is up, including from backups and cloud services where practical. Cover customer data after contract end and data held by suppliers. Keep evidence of what was deleted. Auditors frequently find data kept forever by default.
questions: How long do you keep each type of information?
How is deletion carried out and verified?
How do you handle customer data at contract end?
What about copies in backups and suppliers?
evidence: Deletion logs or automated deletion rules

requirements.title: Data masking
requirements.purpose: Hide or replace sensitive values so people see only what they need.
requirements.guidance: Decide where real values are not needed, for example in support screens, reports, logs and non-production copies, and mask, truncate or tokenise them there. Apply rules consistently and test that masking cannot be easily reversed. Tie it to your data classification and privacy obligations. Check logs for accidental capture of personal data.
questions: Where do you mask or hide sensitive data?
How do you decide which fields are masked?
Do logs or test data contain real personal data?
How do you verify masking works?
evidence: Log review showing no sensitive values

requirements.title: Data leakage prevention
requirements.purpose: Detect and stop sensitive information leaving the organisation without authority.
requirements.guidance: Identify where sensitive data lives and the routes it could leak by, such as email, uploads, cloud sharing and removable media. Use tools or settings like sharing restrictions, email rules and blocking of personal storage to reduce those routes. Monitor alerts and follow up. Pair with training, since most leaks are by mistake.
questions: Which data is most sensitive and where does it sit?
What routes could it leave by?
What controls detect or block unauthorised transfer?
How are alerts followed up?
evidence: Data leakage prevention rules or settings

requirements.title: Information backup
requirements.purpose: Be able to restore information and systems after loss, corruption or attack.
requirements.guidance: Define what is backed up, how often and how long it is kept, based on how much data loss the business can accept. Include system images, configuration and software as well as data, and confirm who backs up the cloud services you depend on. Keep copies separate from the main environment and protected from tampering, such as immutable or offline copies, and encrypt them. Test restores of real systems on a schedule and record how long they took and what failed. Auditors commonly find backups running but never tested.
questions: What is backed up, including systems and configuration, and how often?
Where are backups stored and who can change or delete them?
Which systems were in the most recent restore test, and what did it show?
How do backup frequency and retention meet your recovery targets?
How is data held in software as a service products backed up?
evidence: Backup job success and failure reports
Restore test log with timings and issues
Backup storage access and immutability settings
Provider backup terms for cloud services

requirements.title: Redundancy of information processing facilities
requirements.purpose: Keep critical services running when a component or site fails.
requirements.guidance: Identify services that must stay available and design in spare capacity, such as multiple availability zones, failover databases or a second internet line. Test failover so you know it works. Match the investment to the importance of the service and agreed recovery targets. For cloud hosts, review the provider options and your own configuration.
questions: Which services need redundancy and why?
What failover is in place?
When was failover last tested?
How does redundancy support recovery targets?

requirements.title: Logging
requirements.purpose: Record what happens on systems so activity can be investigated and proven.
requirements.guidance: Decide which events to log, such as sign-ins, admin actions, access to sensitive data, errors and security tool alerts, and send them to a central place. Protect logs from change or deletion, including by the administrators whose actions they record, and keep them for a period set by legal, contract and investigation needs. Analyse logs, with tooling or by review, rather than only storing them, and limit personal data in logs to what is needed. Auditors look for logging gaps on key systems and unrestricted access to logs.
questions: Which events are logged on key systems, and how was that decided?
How are logs protected from alteration by the administrators they record?
How long are logs kept, and why that period?
How are logs analysed, and by whom?
Can you reconstruct a recent event end to end from the logs?
evidence: Logging standard listing events per system
Retention and immutability settings on the log store

requirements.title: Monitoring activities
requirements.purpose: Notice unusual behaviour on systems and networks so you can respond early.
requirements.guidance: Define what normal looks like and set alerts for signs of trouble such as repeated failed sign-ins, unusual data transfers or new admin accounts. Assign someone to review alerts and record what they do. Use provider tools in the cloud. Review the rules as your systems change.
questions: What do you monitor and why?
Who reviews alerts and how fast?
How do you tune alerts to reduce noise?
Can you show a monitored event that led to action?

requirements.title: Clock synchronisation
requirements.purpose: Keep system times consistent so logs can be trusted and compared.
requirements.guidance: Configure all servers, devices and cloud services to use the same reliable time sources. Check for drift on key systems and fix it. Consistent time is essential when piecing together events across systems. This is usually a one-off setup, then a periodic check.
questions: Which time source do your systems use?
How do you check devices stay in sync?
Do logs from different systems line up?
Who owns this configuration?
evidence: Time source configuration for servers and network devices
Time settings for endpoints and cloud services
Correlated log extract from two systems

requirements.title: Use of privileged utility programs
requirements.purpose: Control tools that can bypass normal security checks.
requirements.guidance: Identify utilities that can override controls, such as disk editors, database admin tools and remote administration software. Restrict them to named authorised people, require sign-in and log use. Remove ones not needed. Review the list when systems change.
questions: Which tools could bypass security controls?
Who is authorised to use them?
How is their use logged and reviewed?
How do you stop unauthorised installation?
evidence: List of privileged utilities and owners
Access restriction settings for those utilities
Periodic review of the utility list and authorised users

requirements.title: Installation of software on operational systems
requirements.purpose: Prevent unapproved or untested software from reaching live systems.
requirements.guidance: Allow only approved software on production, installed by authorised people through a controlled process. Test updates first, keep a rollback plan and record versions. Block users from installing their own applications on managed devices. Keep an inventory so you can find unsupported items.
questions: Who can install software on live systems?
How is software approved and tested?
How do you track versions and licences?
What is the rollback plan?

requirements.title: Networks security
requirements.purpose: Protect the network and devices on it from attack and misuse.
requirements.guidance: Document your network, use firewalls with deny-by-default rules and keep device firmware updated. Secure wireless with strong encryption and separate guests. Restrict administrative access to network equipment and review rules regularly. Auditors ask for diagrams and firewall rule reviews.
questions: How is your network protected from outside threats?
How are firewall rules approved and reviewed?
How is wireless secured?
Is there a current network diagram?

requirements.title: Security of network services
requirements.purpose: Make sure the services your network depends on, from ISPs to cloud connectivity, meet your security needs.
requirements.guidance: Identify network services you rely on, whether provided in-house or by suppliers, and define the security and availability you need from them. Put these into contracts or service agreements and monitor performance. Check the supplier security features such as encryption and filtering. Revisit when you change providers.
questions: Which network services do you rely on?
What security requirements have you set?
Are they in contracts or agreements?
How do you monitor service performance?

requirements.title: Segregation of networks
requirements.purpose: Split the network into zones so a problem in one place does not spread.
requirements.guidance: Separate areas such as staff, guests, servers, development and sensitive systems using VLANs, subnets or cloud security groups, with rules controlling traffic between them. Keep guest and personal device Wi-Fi apart from internal systems. Review rules and test that segregation works.
questions: How is your network divided into zones?
What controls traffic between zones?
Are guests and personal devices kept separate?
How do you test the separation?

requirements.title: Web filtering
requirements.purpose: Reduce exposure to harmful or inappropriate websites.
requirements.guidance: Use a filtering service or DNS protection to block known malicious and unwanted categories, and apply it to remote devices as well as the office. Define what is blocked, how exceptions are requested and how people are told. Review reports for patterns. Balance protection against legitimate work needs.
questions: How do you block malicious websites?
Does filtering apply to remote devices?
How are exceptions handled?
Do you review filtering reports?

requirements.title: Use of cryptography
requirements.purpose: Use encryption and key protection properly so data stays confidential and intact.
requirements.guidance: Set rules for where encryption is required, covering data in transit and at rest, and choose recognised, current algorithms. Manage keys carefully, covering generation, storage, rotation and retirement, ideally with a managed key service. Do not store keys alongside the data. Auditors look for expired certificates and unencrypted laptops or databases.
questions: Where do you require encryption and why?
How are encryption keys created, stored and rotated?
How do you manage certificates and their expiry?
Who has access to keys?

requirements.title: Secure development life cycle
requirements.purpose: Build security into how software is made from the start.
requirements.guidance: Define a development process that includes security at each stage: requirements, design, coding, review, testing and release. Keep rules for secure working in the development environment and train developers. Record the approach so it can be shown to customers and auditors. Keep it light enough that teams actually follow it.
questions: How is security built into your development process?
Where in the pipeline are security checks performed?
How are developers trained?
How do you show the process is followed?

requirements.title: Application security requirements
requirements.purpose: Decide up front what security an application must have.
requirements.guidance: For each new or changed application, capture security needs early, covering sign-in, access rules, data protection, logging and resilience, plus legal duties. Base them on risk and data sensitivity. Where the application handles orders, payments or other transactions over networks, add requirements for complete and unaltered transactions, protection of payment data and proof of who did what. Include requirements when buying software or subscribing to a service, not just when building it. Check them at acceptance.
questions: How do you define security requirements for applications?
Who approves them?
How do they cover purchased software and cloud services?
What extra requirements apply to applications that handle transactions or payments?
How do you verify they were met?

requirements.title: Secure system architecture and engineering principles
requirements.purpose: Design systems on sound security principles rather than adding security as an afterthought.
requirements.guidance: Adopt principles such as least privilege, defence in depth, secure defaults and fail safe, and apply them in design reviews. Document reference architectures and review them when technology changes. Apply them to cloud and third-party integrations. Show how a recent design decision used them.
questions: Which security design principles do you follow?
How are they applied in design reviews?
Can you show a design that reflects them?
How do you update the principles?

requirements.title: Secure coding
requirements.purpose: Write code that avoids common weaknesses.
requirements.guidance: Set coding standards that address common flaws, use peer review, static analysis and dependency checks, and avoid exposing secrets. Keep libraries updated and vetted. Train developers on common attack types. Track findings to closure. Auditors sample pull requests and scan results.
questions: What secure coding standards do you use?
How is code reviewed and scanned?
How do you manage third-party libraries?
How do you keep secrets out of code?
evidence: Static analysis and dependency scan results

requirements.title: Security testing in development and acceptance
requirements.purpose: Check security works before software goes live.
requirements.guidance: Plan security tests as part of development, such as automated scans, code review and periodic penetration testing, and set acceptance criteria. Test in an environment close to production. Fix or formally accept findings before release. Keep results.
questions: What security testing do you perform before release?
Who decides if findings block a release?
How do you test in realistic conditions?
How are results tracked?

requirements.title: Outsourced development
requirements.purpose: Keep control of security when others build software for you.
requirements.guidance: Set security requirements in contracts, including coding standards, testing, confidentiality and ownership of the code. Review the supplier practices and check deliverables for flaws. Control their access to your systems and remove it afterwards. Keep rights to the source code or escrow arrangements where needed.
questions: How do you set security requirements for outsourced developers?
How do you check the quality and security of delivered code?
What access do suppliers have to your systems?
Who owns the code?
evidence: Code review or test records for deliveries

requirements.title: Separation of development, test and production environments
requirements.purpose: Keep experimental work away from live systems and data.
requirements.guidance: Use separate environments for development, testing and production, with different access rights and no direct path from development to live. Do not use real personal data in non-production unless protected. Promote changes through a controlled pipeline. Check developers do not hold standing production access.
questions: How are your environments separated?
Who has access to each environment?
How do changes move to production?
Is real data used in test?

requirements.title: Change management
requirements.purpose: Make changes to systems in a controlled way so they do not cause outages or weaken security.
requirements.guidance: Require changes to be requested, assessed, approved, tested and recorded, with a rollback plan. Use lighter paths for low-risk routine changes and faster emergency routes that are reviewed afterwards. Keep a change log and check it against reality. Auditors sample changes and look for approvals and testing.
questions: How are changes requested and approved?
How do you handle urgent changes?
How do you test and roll back?
Can you show records for recent changes?

requirements.title: Test information
requirements.purpose: Protect the data used for testing.
requirements.guidance: Avoid using live personal or confidential data in testing. Prefer synthetic or anonymised data, and if real data is unavoidable, protect it as in production, limit access and delete it after use. Record approvals. Check that test copies are not left lying around.
questions: What data do you use for testing?
How is real data approved and protected if used?
How is test data removed afterwards?
Who can access test data?
evidence: Approvals for use of live data

requirements.title: Protection of information systems during audit testing
requirements.purpose: Make sure audits and technical checks do not disrupt or expose live systems.
requirements.guidance: Plan and agree the scope, timing and method of any testing with the owner of the system beforehand. Give auditors read-only access where possible, remove it afterwards and avoid tests that could damage live data. Back up first for intrusive checks. Record what was accessed.
questions: How are audit tests on live systems agreed?
What access do auditors get and how is it removed?
How do you avoid disruption?
How is audit access logged?
